analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $4.70 an hour, then to $5.15.
analysis.headline: A minimum wage increase to $4.70 and then $5.15 an hour, backed by 118 House cosponsors, was referred to a committee and never received a vote before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise the federal minimum wage from $4.25 an hour to $4.70 starting in mid-1995, and to $5.15 after mid-1996 [S2][S3]. It was introduced by Rep. Richard Gephardt with a long list of original cosponsors and quickly drew 118 cosponsors in total [S3][S4]. It was referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities and then to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it stayed; no committee vote and no floor vote ever occurred, and the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 with the bill dead [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage would see their hourly pay rise to $4.70 and then $5.15, a roughly 21% increase over two years from the $4.25 baseline [S2][S3]. Households relying on that paycheck, disproportionately in food service, retail, and other low-wage work, would gain directly.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $4.70 an hour during the year beginning July 4, 1995 [S2][S3].
Raises it again to $5.15 an hour after July 3, 1996, about 21% above the $4.25 rate then in effect [S2][S3].
The increase applies nationally under the Fair Labor Standards Act, covering workers whose pay floor is set by federal law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum wage would bear the higher payroll, most directly restaurants, retail stores, and small businesses with many entry-level workers. Some of that cost would likely be passed to customers through prices, and some employers might respond by cutting hours or slowing hiring at the bottom of the wage scale.

drawbacks.text: Mandated raises raise labor costs for employers with many minimum-wage workers; small businesses and franchise restaurants argued such increases squeeze margins and can lead to reduced hours, automation, or fewer entry-level jobs.
The increase is uniform nationwide, so the same $5.15 floor carries more weight in low-cost rural areas than in high-wage cities, which opponents said fits some regions poorly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the benefit is straightforward and substantial: a roughly 21% raise in the legal pay floor over two years, at a time when the minimum wage had not been raised since 1991. The cost falls on a different group, the businesses that employ them, and the strongest honest objection is that some of that cost shows up in prices, reduced hours, or slower hiring for the very workers the bill targets. On balance the trade favors low-wage workers, which is why the main fight was over whether the bill would ever reach a vote, not over the size of the increase.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: referred to the House education and labor committee and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed without ever getting a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gephardt introduced the bill on February 14, 1995 with dozens of original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities [S3][S5].
The bill drew 118 cosponsors, 116 Democrats and 2 Independents [S4].

On March 3, 1995 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections; no further action was recorded, and no committee or floor vote ever took place before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers are better off, because the higher pay floor never arrived. The committee and subcommittee that received the bill also avoided a vote on a measure with broad cosponsorship.

for.name: Rep. Richard Gephardt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited dozens of original cosponsors on day one.

for.name: 116 House Democrats and 2 Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 118 cosponsors in total.

against.name: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 3, 1995 and took no further recorded action.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House floor schedule in 1995-96 and did not bring the bill up for a vote while the minimum wage increase stayed in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 118 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents and none were Republicans; opposition came through the Republican-controlled committee structure rather than a recorded vote.

industries.note: Among the most minimum-wage-intensive industries, it would have paid the full increase; blocking the bill kept payroll costs down at the price of workers' raises.
Large retail employers with many entry-level workers would have absorbed higher payroll; the bill's defeat preserved their cost structure.
Owners would have faced the same higher wage floor; opponents argued the increase squeezed small operations hardest.
The group the bill was written for lost the chance at a 21% raise in the federal pay floor.
